title: I'm not doing 996.
author: Elena Verna
summary: Elena Verna, who works at the fast-growing AI company Lovable and is the mother of two, argues against the 996 culture (9am to 9pm, six days a week) spreading through AI companies. She says willingness to work insane hours is not the same as ambition, commitment or talent, and that 996 borrows from employees' future health and relationships in a debt that never appears on a balance sheet. Normalizing it also screens out parents, caregivers and experienced people who would improve the product. She describes her own boundaries and offers three principles: stop chasing work-life balance in favor of recognizing the season you are in, apply a five-year regret test, and say boundaries out loud. She tells leaders that their own behavior sets the real standard, and closes by saying the future of work is still a choice.
points: Verna distinguishes sprinting when a launch or emergency demands it from designing an organization where everyone sprints forever, and says needing 996 to win points to a prioritization failure.
Normalizing 996 filters out parents, caregivers and experienced people, while constraints outside work can make someone a better operator by forcing ruthless prioritization.
Companies must make boundaries safe for junior staff, but she warns that nobody will protect your time but you, since someone will always find as many hours of problems as you are willing to give.
Her five-year regret test asks which choice you will regret more later, and she notes that her regrets almost always come from missing family, not work.
Leaders set the real standard through what they do and reward, so midnight messages and visible overwork undercut any wellness policy.
quotes: There’s a big difference between working hard with working all the time.
You’re getting more output today by consuming someone’s future health, relationships, and capacity to perform.
But there’s a difference between sprinting when you really need to and designing an org where everyone is expected to sprint all the time, forever.

The actual test of a company’s commitment to sustainable working practices isn’t whether the top execs can leave early to pick up their kids. It’s whether junior employees feel they can do the same without sacrificing their careers.
If you’re willing to give your company 12 hours, I promise someone will find 12 hours of problems for you to solve.

So now, when I’m really torn between a work commitment and something personal, I try to mentally remove myself from the immediate situation and ask: Which decision am I more likely to regret 5 years from now?
People pay attention to what gets rewarded, not just what gets said.
I actually think having constraints outside work makes you a better operator.
